title: Dynamic models: state machines + activity diagrams
intro: L6's dynamic models: state machine notation (states, entry/do/exit, event[guard]/action, start/end), dialog maps for UI navigation, and activity diagrams (fork/join, decision/merge, swimlanes), with the Tutorial 3 projector worked through.

cards.title: What a state is
cards.body:
A state machine diagram (statechart, finite state automaton) models a system or object by the **states** it can be in (L6 slide 3).
A **state** is a stable condition that lasts for a period of time (or forever) until some action drives the system into another stable state.
Example: a 2-bit counter has 4 states, 00 → 01 → 10 → 11 → 00, moved on by a clock signal.
keypoints: State = stable condition that lasts
Events/actions move the system between states
Name states as conditions (Off, Warming Up), never as button presses

cards.title: State notation
cards.body:
A state is a **rounded rectangle**: name at the top, optionally a description and internal actions (L6 slide 4):
- `entry / action`: done once on entering
- `exit / action`: done once on leaving
- `do / activity`: ongoing while in the state
A diagram starts at a **start node** (filled dot), goes through states and transitions, and ends at an **end node** (bullseye), **unless the system loops forever**, in which case there is no end node (L6 slide 5).
cards.diagram:
stateDiagram-v2
[*] --> StateName
StateName : entry / action
StateName : exit / action
StateName : do / activity
StateName --> [*]
keypoints: entry = once in; exit = once out; do = while in
Start node = filled dot; end node = bullseye
End node is optional for systems that never stop

cards.title: Transitions: event(args)[guard]/action
cards.body:
A transition is **instantaneous**, in response to an event (L6 slide 5). Its label has three optional parts:
- **event**: what triggers it, e.g. `insert(c:Coin)`
- **[guard]**: a condition that must be true to take it, e.g. `[amount is enough for i]`
- **/action**: done during the transition, e.g. `/ dispense(i)`
Full form: `event(arguments)[guard]/action`.
keypoints: Event = trigger; [guard] = boolean condition; /action = work done
All three are optional (guard-only and unlabelled transitions are legal)
A button press is an event, never a [guard]

cards.title: Worked example: vending machine (L6 slide 7)
cards.body:
Read it like a marker would:
- The start arrow is labelled `Power On / Reset`, and **Power Off** leads to the end node.
- **Idle**: entry sets amount to 0, do displays a greeting.
- `insert(c)` → **Accumulate**. A **self-transition** on `insert(c)` re-enters it, so the entry action adds each new coin.
- `select(i)[amount enough for i]` → **Vend** (entry subtracts the cost, do dispenses).
- Guard-only exits: `[amount = 0]` → Idle, `[amount > 0]` → **ReturnChange** → Idle (unlabelled).
cards.diagram:
stateDiagram-v2
[*] --> Idle : Power On / Reset
Idle : entry / amount = 0
Idle : do / display(greeting)
Idle --> Accumulate : insert(c)
Accumulate : entry / amount = amount + c.amount
Accumulate : do / display(amount)
Accumulate --> Accumulate : insert(c)
Accumulate --> Vend : select(i) [amount enough for i]
Vend : entry / amount = amount - i.cost
Vend : do / dispense(i)
Vend --> Idle : [amount = 0]
Vend --> ReturnChange : [amount > 0]
ReturnChange : do / return(amount)
ReturnChange --> Idle
Idle --> [*] : Power Off
cards.after: The slide writes `amount := 0`. Here `=` is used only because of the renderer.
keypoints: Self-transition re-runs the entry action
Mutually exclusive guards choose the exit
The slide calls this a dialog map

cards.title: Dialog maps
cards.body:
Many UIs behave like finite state machines: **one screen/window active at a time = a state**, and defined conditions for moving between screens = transitions. This is a **dialog map** (L6 slide 6).
Used with **prototyping** (which reduces the risk of building the wrong product, or the right product badly), it lets users try the navigation and preview each screen's functions.
Benefits (slide 6):
- find **missing or incorrect navigation pathways** early, when they are cheap to fix
- spot **reuse and redundancies** in the UI
- without worrying about screen design details too early
Example (L6 slide 8): Students List → add new → Personal Info Form → next/back → Academic Info Form → next/back → Activity Info Form → save; cancel goes back.
keypoints: Dialog map = state machine whose states are screens
Its job: catch missing/incorrect navigation early
Every screen needs a way out (cancel/back), so check for dead ends

cards.title: Practice: stopwatch (L6 slide 9)
cards.body:
Ready (entry / Reset time) → **Click Start** → Continuous Update (do / Display time elapsed) → **Click Stop** → Time Paused. From Time Paused: **Click Start** → Continuous Update, **Click Reset** → Ready. **Click Close Window** from any state → end node.
The time is reset by Ready's **entry action**, so every arrival in Ready resets it.
cards.diagram:
stateDiagram-v2
[*] --> Ready
Ready : entry / Reset time
Ready --> ContinuousUpdate : Click Start
ContinuousUpdate : do / Display time elapsed
ContinuousUpdate --> TimePaused : Click Stop
TimePaused --> ContinuousUpdate : Click Start
TimePaused --> Ready : Click Reset
Ready --> [*] : Click Close Window
ContinuousUpdate --> [*] : Click Close Window
TimePaused --> [*] : Click Close Window
keypoints: Events with no outgoing transition from the current state are not handled by the model
Reset only works from Time Paused here
Put a repeated action in the target state's entry instead of on every arrow

cards.title: Worked: projector state machine (Tutorial 3 Q2)
cards.body:
Scenario: turn on → warms up (beep once, red light blinks) → when ready, light turns green and input defaults to PC → Jane presses LAPTOP. OFF turns it off, but Jane leaves it on.
Model answer:
1. Find states (stable conditions): **Off, Warming Up, Ready (PC input), Projecting Laptop**.
2. Events: press ON, warm-up complete, press LAPTOP, press OFF.
3. Internal actions: Warming Up has `entry / beep` and `do / blink red light`. Ready has `entry / light green`.
4. No end node: the projector cycles (OFF → Off → ON tomorrow), which is the infinite-loop case (L6 slide 5). 'Leaves it ON' just means staying in Projecting Laptop.
cards.diagram:
stateDiagram-v2
state "Warming Up" as WarmingUp
state "Ready (PC input)" as ReadyPC
state "Projecting Laptop" as Laptop
[*] --> Off
Off --> WarmingUp : press ON
WarmingUp : entry / beep
WarmingUp : do / blink red light
WarmingUp --> ReadyPC : warm-up complete
ReadyPC : entry / light green
ReadyPC --> Laptop : press LAPTOP
ReadyPC --> Off : press OFF
Laptop --> Off : press OFF
cards.after: No official solution exists. 'warm-up complete' could also be written as a guard such as `[warmed up]`. Either is fine if it's explained.
keypoints: Button presses go on transitions, not in state names
Beep = entry action (once); blinking = do activity (ongoing)
No end node is needed for a device that cycles forever
Optional, if you state the assumption: press PC from Laptop back to Ready (PC input); press OFF from Warming Up

cards.title: Activity diagram notation (L6 slide 10)
cards.body:
- **Activity**: execution of one or more basic operations, drawn as a rounded rectangle
- **Control flow**: arrows between activities
- **Fork**: one input, two or more outputs, so the activities run **concurrently** (bar)
- **Join**: two or more flows come together into one (bar)
- **Decision** (branch): flow goes ONE of several ways depending on a condition (diamond + `[guards]`)
- **Merge**: several branches back into one (diamond)
- Start = filled dot, end = bullseye. **Swimlanes** = columns per participant (L6 slide 15).
keypoints: Fork/join = concurrency (bars)
Decision/merge = choice (diamonds)
Guards on decision exits: [valid PIN] / [invalid PIN], [still wet] / [else]

cards.title: Worked: Do Laundry + Dry Clothes (L6 slides 11-12)
cards.body:
**Do Laundry**: Sort Clothes → **fork** → Wash Whites ∥ Wash Darks → **join** → Dry Clothes (a sub-activity, marked with the rake icon) → end.
**Dry Clothes**: start → **merge** → Run Dryer → **decision**: `[still wet]` loops back to the merge, `[else]` → Fold Clothes → end.
cards.diagram:
flowchart TD
S((start)) --> A([Sort clothes into whites and darks])
A --> F["FORK bar"]
F --> W1([Wash whites])
F --> W2([Wash darks])
W1 --> J["JOIN bar"]
W2 --> J
J --> M{merge}
M --> R([Run dryer])
R --> D{decision}
D -->|"[still wet]"| M
D -->|"[else]"| FO([Fold clothes])
FO --> E((end))
style F fill:#222,color:#fff
style J fill:#222,color:#fff
cards.after: Here Dry Clothes is expanded inline. On the slides it is a separate diagram.
keypoints: Concurrency → fork + join
Loop → decision + merge (never fork/join)
A sub-activity can be expanded in its own diagram

cards.title: Worked: swimlanes, ATM (L6 slide 15)
cards.body:
Lanes: **Customer | ATM Machine | Bank**.
Customer: Insert card → Enter pin → Bank: Authorize → **branch** `[valid PIN]` → Enter amount → Bank: Check account balance → branch `[balance >= amount]` → **fork** → Take money from slot (Customer) ∥ Debit account (Bank) → **join** → Show balance → **merge** (with the `[invalid PIN]` and `[balance < amount]` paths) → Eject card → Take card → end.
Other slides (13, 14) show the same ideas: Sales/Consultant/Technician lanes with decisions; a two-start-node example where a join waits for Sarah's 'Start process' and the server's success path.
cards.diagram:
flowchart TD
subgraph Customer
I([Insert card]) --> P([Enter pin])
EA([Enter amount])
T([Take money])
TC([Take card])
end
subgraph Bank
AU([Authorize]) --> D1{PIN ok?}
CB([Check balance]) --> D2{enough?}
DB([Debit account])
end
subgraph ATM
F["FORK"]
J["JOIN"] --> SB([Show balance]) --> M{merge}
M --> EJ([Eject card])
end
P --> AU
D1 -->|"[valid PIN]"| EA --> CB
D1 -->|"[invalid PIN]"| M
D2 -->|"[balance >= amount]"| F
D2 -->|"[balance < amount]"| M
F --> T --> J
F --> DB --> J
EJ --> TC
cards.after: Simplified from the slide (the slide has an extra merge before Show balance).
keypoints: Put each activity in the lane of whoever does it
Failure paths rejoin via a merge, not a join
Label every decision exit with a guard

cards.title: State machine vs activity diagram
cards.body:
**Activity diagram**: a flow chart of activities. It describes the **workflow** behaviour of the system (L6 slide 16).
**State machine**: models a system/object by the **states** it can be in.
Which one to use:
- 'What screens/modes does it have and what moves it between them?' → state machine / dialog map
- 'What steps happen, in what order, by whom, with what decisions or parallel work?' → activity diagram (+ swimlanes)
Both are dynamic models of requirements analysis (L5 slide 4, L6). L6 slide 18 shows the whole elicitation-and-analysis process itself as an activity diagram (study spec → use cases → review → identify classes → add associations and dynamic diagrams → review → sign off SRS).
keypoints: Boxes in a state machine = conditions; boxes in an activity diagram = work
Object lifecycle → state machine; process/workflow → activity
Both belong to the dynamic model

cards.title: Traps the marker penalises
cards.body:
- **States named after events** ('Press LAPTOP'). States are conditions; presses go on arrows.
- **Event written as a guard** (`[press OFF]`). Guards are conditions; events are triggers.
- Splitting one condition into several states ('Beep', 'Blink'). Use entry/do inside one state.
- Adding an **end node to a device that cycles forever**, or forgetting one when the system really does stop (Power Off, Close Window).
- **Fork used for a choice**. Use a decision diamond.
- **Join after a decision**: it deadlocks, so use a merge.
- Unlabelled decision exits: every branch needs a `[guard]`.
- Dialog map with **dead ends** (no cancel/back).
keypoints: States = conditions, events = arrows
[guard] = boolean
Fork/join ↔ concurrency, decision/merge ↔ choice

cards.title: Exam recipe
cards.body:
**State machine / dialog map from a narrative:**
1. List the stable conditions (or the screens) → states.
2. List the triggers (button presses, signals, timeouts) → events.
3. Conditions that must also hold → `[guards]`. Things done → `/action` on the arrow, or entry/do/exit inside the state.
4. Draw the start node to the first state. Add an end node only if the system really stops.
5. For every state ask: 'what can happen here?' Add the missing arrows, e.g. cancel/back, OFF (state assumptions).
**Activity diagram from a use case:**
1. One swimlane per actor/system part.
2. Steps → activities in the right lane.
3. Alternatives → decision with `[guards]`, rejoined by a merge.
4. Parallel steps → fork ... join.
5. Start node, end node.
keypoints: Label format: event(args)[guard]/action
Check each state for a missing transition
Check every bar and diamond: is it concurrency or choice?
